analysis.note: The final visarga is lost before the following e of enam: yaḥ + enam → ya enam.
The accusative pronoun refers to the embodied Self under discussion.
Predicative accusative with enam: ‘as the killer.’
Visarga becomes ś before ca: yaḥ + ca → yaś ca.
This shares the printed orthographic span cainaṃ with the following enam: ca + enam → cainam.
This shares the printed orthographic span cainaṃ with preceding ca.
Although the form has Ātmanepada endings, its construction is active: the relative pronoun is the one who forms the judgment.
A kta-derived adjective used as a predicative accusative with enam: ‘as slain.’
The canonical nominal stem is ubha, not the verbal root ubh.
Correlative with the two preceding yaḥ clauses.
The final -aḥ becomes -o before the following voiced n: vijānītaḥ na → vijānīto na. The understood object is the Self.
This shares the printed orthographic span nāyaṃ with the following ayam: na + ayam → nāyam.
This shares the printed orthographic span nāyaṃ with preceding na and denotes the Self.
Active construction whose agency is denied of the Self.
Passive: the Self is denied the status of the object affected by killing.

justifications.decision: Both occurrences of enam and the later ayam denote the embodied Self (ātman) under discussion, not the physical body.
Hantāram is a predicative accusative construed with enam and means ‘as the killer,’ specifically the agent of the act of killing.
options_considered: predicative accusative, ‘knows this as the killer’

evidence.translation: ‘the killer, the agent of the act of killing’

justifications.decision: Manyate is active in construction, and hatam is its predicative accusative: the second person mistakenly considers the Self to be slain because the body has been killed.

evidence.quote: ya ca enam anyo manyate hataṃ deha-hananena hato 'ham iti hanana-kriyāyāḥ karma-bhūtam
evidence.translation: ‘and another who considers this slain—“I have been slain” through the killing of the body—as the object of the act of killing’

evidence.quote: hantā ahaṃ, hato 'smy aham iti deha-hananena ātmānam
evidence.translation: ‘[those who apprehend] the Self, through the killing of the body, as “I am the killer” or “I have been slain”’

justifications.decision: Ubhau tau correlates with the two yaḥ clauses. The negative means that neither of those two possesses true knowledge of the Self; ātmānam is the understood object of vijānītaḥ.
options_considered: ‘both know nothing’ without a specified object
‘neither of those two understands the Self’
‘the two do not recognize each other’
justifications.chosen: ‘neither of those two understands the Self’

evidence.quote: tau ubhau na vijānītaḥ na jñātavantau avivekena ātmānam
evidence.translation: ‘Those two both do not understand—have not known—the Self, owing to nondiscrimination.’

evidence.quote: yau vijānītaḥ tau ātma-svarūpānabhijñau ity arthaḥ
evidence.translation: ‘Those two who apprehend it thus are ignorant of the Self’s true nature: that is the meaning.’

justifications.decision: Hanti is active and hanyate passive, but the verse denies that the immutable Self is respectively the agent or the affected object of killing.
options_considered: a claim only that the Self survives death
a denial of both agency and object-status in killing
justifications.chosen: denial that the Self is either killing-agent or killed object, grounded in its immutability

evidence.quote: hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ, avikriyatvāt
evidence.translation: ‘It does not kill: it does not become the agent of the act of killing; nor is it killed, nor does it become the object—that is the meaning—because it is immutable.’

justifications.decision: The lemma of ubhau is the nominal stem ubha, rather than the verbal root ubh proposed as the stem by Vyākaraṇī.

translation:
Whoever knows this Self (ātman) as the killer,
and whoever considers it slain—
neither of those two understands:
this Self does not kill, nor is it killed.
one_shot_delta: A commentary-blind translation might leave enam as an ambiguous ‘him’; Śaṅkara identifies its referent as the embodied Self, not the body.
It might miss that hantāram and hatam are predicative accusatives assigning the Self the roles of killing-agent and killed object.
It might treat bodily death as the Self’s death; the commentary explains ‘I have been slain’ as a mistaken identification produced by the killing of the body.
It might render the final line merely as a paradox or ethical prohibition, whereas Śaṅkara takes it as a denial of agency and object-status based on the Self’s immutability.
analyzer_disagreements: For ubhau, Vyākaraṇī gives the stem ubh. This is overridden by the supplied canonical lemma ubha; ubh is a verbal root, whereas ubhau is the masculine nominative dual of the nominal ubha.
open_questions: The plaintext has atmā in commentary line 4, evidently an unmarked or defective transcription of ātmā; the interpretation is independently secured by ātmānam in lines 2–3.
Because cainaṃ and nāyaṃ each represent two morphologically segmented words in one orthographic sandhi span, that complete printed span is recorded for both participating analyses.
mula: ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaś cainaṃ manyate hatam | ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate
commentary_lines: ya enaṃ prakṛtaṃ dehinaṃ vetti vijānāti hantāraṃ hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartāraṃ ya ca enam anyo manyate hataṃ deha-hananena hato 'ham iti hanana-kriyāyāḥ karma-bhūtam |
tau ubhau na vijānītaḥ na jñātavantau avivekena ātmānam |
hantā ahaṃ, hato 'smy aham iti deha-hananena ātmānam ahaṃ pratyaya-viṣayaṃ yau vijānītaḥ tau ātma-svarūpānabhijñau ity arthaḥ |
yasmāt na ayam atmā hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ, avikriyatvāt ||bhgs_2.19||
